range.content: When the soul of a man is born in this country there are nets flung at it to hold it back from flight. You talk to me of nationality, language, religion. I shall try to fly by those nets

children: There are two interpretations for what this passage could mean, specifically the third last word: “by”.

The obvious is that Dedalus will try to “fly” past the nets of “nationality, language, and religion” which have restrained him or his “soul” since birth. He will fly by them in that he will evade and escape them, flourishing as an artist and a person in spite of their restrictive powers.

However, there is an alternative understanding of this phrase. Dedalus could mean that he intends to fly by these nets in that it is by use of nets that he will fly. It will not be in spite of, but with these nets which have constrained him all of his life that he will soar above his entrapment.

This is implicit in the way in which Dedalus has grown as a writer and as a person throughout the text. His narrative, while it has grown past the restrictions of his surroundings, does so entirely through them. Later on in the chapter Cranly remarks “dispassionately”: “It is a curious thing, do you know… how your mind is supersaturated with the religion in which you disbelieve.” This is accurate: while Dedalus entirely rejects his religious upbringing his use of language and his way of thinking are irreversibly coloured by it. Similarly his nationality and his culture have molded him and his art irreversibly.

Through this interpretation of the statement, Dedalus is claiming that he will transcend as a spirit not in spite of his upbringing but with it. It is “by” or because of that which once tied him down that he will ascend.

children: Stephen also rejects Irish nationalism because he feels its people have turned their backs on their own leaders. Wolfe Tone and Charles Stewart Parnell, both prominent Protestant Irish leaders for an Independent Ireland, were betrayed (or at least abandoned) by their own when the chips were down. Tone was a founding member of the United Irishmen, but was eventually caught and imprisoned. He committed suicide before he was due to be executed. Many other United Irishmen met the same fate, such as Henry Joy McCracken, a Presbyterian who was hanged in his own native Belfast. Around this time the United Irishmen had begun to dissolve due to growing issues between Protestants (primarily Ulster Scots Presbyterians who made up the bulk of the movement) and Catholics, who at this time both considered themselves as being Irish. Likewise, when Parnell’s affair was brought to light, many of his supporters abandoned him and turned their back on him. Stephen finds Irish nationalism faulty because he sees its people as being so quick to turn on their own leaders or to let their disagreements eradicate their goals.
